questions.stem: Who was the founder of the Maurya Empire, who overthrew the Nanda dynasty with the help of his mentor Chanakya?

options.option_text: Chandragupta Maurya
Ashoka
Bindusara
Samudragupta

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya Empire around 322 BCE. Guided by his brilliant Brahmin mentor Chanakya (Kautilya), he raised an army, overthrew the unpopular Dhana Nanda of the Nanda Dynasty, and established his capital at Pataliputra (modern Patna). He later defeated Seleucus Nicator, one of Alexander the Great's generals, securing India's northwestern borders.
DECOY BUSTING: Bindusara was his son. Ashoka (the Great) was his grandson. Samudragupta was a famous ruler of the much later Gupta Empire.
EXAM INSIGHT: In his later years, Chandragupta gave up his massive empire, embraced Jainism under the sage Bhadrabahu, and migrated to Shravanabelagola (Karnataka), where he died performing the Jain ritual of 'Sallekhana' (fasting to death).

questions.stem: Emperor Ashoka's famous conversion to Buddhism was deeply influenced by the immense bloodshed he witnessed during the conquest of which region?

options.option_text: Kalinga
Magadha
Gandhara
Taxila

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: In 261 BCE, Emperor Ashoka conquered the independent kingdom of Kalinga (modern-day coastal Odisha). The war was exceptionally brutal, resulting in the deaths of over 100,000 people and the deportation of 150,000 more. Witnessing this horrific bloodshed filled Ashoka with profound remorse. He abandoned his policy of physical conquest ('Bherighosha') in favor of cultural/spiritual conquest ('Dhammaghosha') and embraced Buddhism.
DECOY BUSTING: Magadha was the home state of the Mauryas (their capital). Gandhara and Taxila were provinces already under Mauryan control in the northwest.
EXAM INSIGHT: The horrific details of the Kalinga War and Ashoka's subsequent remorse are vividly documented in his Major Rock Edict XIII, which is the longest and most important of all his edicts.

questions.stem: Which ancient text, authored by Chanakya (Kautilya), serves as a comprehensive manual on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy for the Mauryan administration?

options.option_text: Arthashastra
Indica
Mudrarakshasa
Rajatarangini

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: The 'Arthashastra' (Science of Wealth/Politics) is an ancient Indian Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy. It was authored by Kautilya (also known as Chanakya or Vishnugupta), who was the prime minister and mentor to Chandragupta Maurya. It prescribes highly pragmatic, sometimes ruthless, advice on running an empire, managing spies, and maximizing tax revenue.
DECOY BUSTING: 'Indica' was written by the Greek ambassador Megasthenes. 'Mudrarakshasa' is a later play by Vishakhadatta detailing how Chanakya overthrew the Nandas. 'Rajatarangini' is a historical chronicle of Kashmir by Kalhana.
EXAM INSIGHT: The text was lost for centuries and only dramatically rediscovered in 1905 by R. Shamasastry in a library in Mysore.

questions.stem: The Greek envoy Megasthenes, sent by Seleucus Nicator to the Mauryan court, compiled an invaluable firsthand account of India. By what title is this work known today?

options.option_text: Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (a Greek maritime guide)
Indica (Megasthenes' firsthand account of Mauryan India)
Mudrarakshasa (a Sanskrit play on Chandragupta's rise)
Milindapanha (a dialogue involving Greek king Menander)

questions.explanation: Megasthenes wrote 'Indica', describing Mauryan society, the caste structure, geography, and Chandragupta's court at Pataliputra. The Periplus is a 1st-century CE maritime text by an unknown Greek author — a frequent distractor because both are Greek sources on India, but separated by ~300 years and entirely different in scope.

questions.stem: Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts consistently refer to the emperor using a royal title. What is the title that appears in these inscriptions, meaning 'Beloved of the Gods, of Gracious Mien'?

options.option_text: Chakravartin (universal sovereign of the Mauryan dynasty)
Devanampiya Piyadassi (used in Ashoka's own inscriptions)
Sandrokottos (Greek rendering recorded by Megasthenes' text)
Amitraghata (epithet linked to slaying of enemy kingdoms)

questions.explanation: 'Devanampiya Piyadassi' appears throughout Ashoka's edicts. The identification of this title with Ashoka was confirmed only in 1915 when the Maski edict used the name 'Ashoka Devanampiya' together. 'Sandrokottos' is the Greek name for Chandragupta; 'Amitraghata' is associated with Bindusara.

questions.stem: Bindusara, the second Mauryan emperor, is recorded in Greek sources under a title derived from a Sanskrit epithet meaning 'Slayer of Enemies.' Which of the following is that epithet?

options.option_text: Amitraghata (Sanskrit compound meaning 'destroyer of foes')
Sandrokottos (Greek transliteration of Chandragupta's name)
Priyadarshi (meaning 'of gracious looks', Ashoka's epithet)
Vrishasena (a later title used in Gupta-period inscriptions)

questions.explanation: Greek sources record Bindusara as 'Amitrochates', a phonetic rendering of Sanskrit 'Amitraghata' (destroyer of enemies). Candidates frequently confuse this with Ashoka's epithets (Priyadarshi, Devanampiya) or with Chandragupta's Greek name Sandrokottos — both are plausible-sounding distractors from the same dynasty.

questions.stem: Ashoka's inscriptions are found in multiple scripts across the subcontinent. The Kharosthi-script versions of his edicts were concentrated in which specific region?

options.option_text: Eastern coastal belt covering Bengal and Odisha provinces
Northwestern frontier areas in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan
Southern Deccan plateau in present-day Andhra and Karnataka
Central India along the Narmada valley and Vindhya ranges

questions.explanation: Kharosthi was the native script of the northwestern subcontinent. Ashokan edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra (both in modern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan) are inscribed in Kharosthi. All other regions used Brahmi. Candidates often place them in the south because Ashoka had significant Buddhist activity there — a classic misdirection.

questions.stem: Ashoka created a new cadre of officials called 'Dhamma Mahamattas' (Dharma Superintendents), first mentioned in Rock Edict V. What was the core mandate assigned to them?

options.option_text: Auditing provincial revenue accounts and preventing tax evasion
Supervising construction of Buddhist viharas and stupa projects
Propagating Dhamma and ensuring welfare across all communities
Running the imperial intelligence network to monitor provinces

questions.explanation: Rock Edict V records Ashoka creating Dhamma Mahamattas to work among all sects, caring for prisoners, the aged, women in royal harems, and frontier peoples. They were welfare-cum-missionary officials, not construction managers — though Ashoka's well-known stupa-building activity makes option B a tempting distractor.

questions.stem: Ashoka's Rock Edict IV mentions empowering a class of officials called 'Rajukas' with a distinctive judicial grant. What specific authority did Rajukas hold that set them apart from ordinary Mauryan revenue officers?

options.option_text: Independent power to reward the virtuous and punish the guilty
Exclusive rights to levy elephant tribute from forest-tribe areas
Command over border garrisons with power to raise emergency levies
Authority to ratify or overturn village-headman (gramika) appointments

questions.explanation: Rock Edict IV explicitly states that Rajukas were placed over many hundred-thousands of people and granted independent (autonomous) power to reward and punish — an unusual decentralisation of judicial-executive authority. They are distinct from Yuktas (subordinate officials) and Mahamattas (senior officers). Candidates confuse them with revenue collectors or military commanders.

questions.stem: The Arthashastra classifies forests by their strategic utility to the Mauryan state. Which category was designated 'Hastivanam' and placed under the strictest state monopoly with settlement and hunting strictly forbidden?

options.option_text: Forests producing sal and teak timber for chariot manufacturing
Forests reserved for capturing and breeding state war elephants
Forests supplying medicinal herbs to the imperial palace dispensary
Forests granted tax-free to Brahmin agrahara settlement colonies

questions.explanation: The Arthashastra designates 'Hastivanam' (elephant forests) as inviolable state reserves because war elephants were a decisive military asset — the Mauryan army's core striking force. A dedicated Hastyadhyaksha (Elephant Superintendent) administered these reserves. Timber forests (Dravyavana) were a separate category with different regulations, making option A a common wrong answer.
